idiom_name: capturing lambda over the bound arguments
implementation_notes: C++11 lambdas are closures: `[add](int y) { return add(5, y); }` stores a copy of the bound callable and values inside the closure object, so a specialisation is an ordinary callable that inlines. The standard library's partial-application machinery - std::bind with placeholders and, since C++20, std::bind_front/bind_back whose invocation is expression-equivalent to std::invoke(f, bound..., call...) - is grouped by cppreference under "Partial function application"; since C++14 generic lambdas and init-capture (`[cfg = std::move(cfg)]`), the lambda is the default and std::bind is kept for code that must name its bound list or forward an overload set that a lambda would have to spell out.
pitfalls: Capture by reference ([&]) of a local that dies before the specialised function is called leaves a dangling reference; capture by value or with an init-capture ([x = x]) makes the lifetime explicit.
A closure type is unnameable: storing it in std::function erases the type (possible allocation, no inlining), and declaring it in a header needs decltype or a type-erased boundary.
Captured state is copied into the closure object, so mutating the original afterwards does not change the specialisation - either the point of the pattern, or a silent surprise.

variants.name: std::bind with placeholders (C++11 library)
variants.implementation_notes: std::bind generates a forwarding call wrapper whose invocation is equivalent to calling f with some arguments bound to args; placeholders _1, _2 ... mark the positions left open, so any argument can be fixed, not only the leading ones. It stores decayed copies of everything passed (wrap deliberate references in std::ref/std::cref) and returns an object for which std::is_bind_expression is true, which nesting must respect. Choose it where the bound list is itself data or where a member pointer must be adapted; prefer a lambda for readable, inlinable specialisations and std::bind_front when only the leading arguments are bound.
pitfalls: bind stores decayed copies: a parameter meant to be bound by reference silently binds a copy unless it is wrapped in std::ref or std::cref.
Overload sets and function templates need an explicit cast or a lambda, because std::bind cannot deduce which overload was meant; nested bind expressions behave specially through is_bind_expression.

variants.name: std::bind_front / std::bind_back (C++20/23)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20's std::bind_front generates a perfect-forwarding call wrapper whose invocation is expression-equivalent to std::invoke(f, bound_args..., call_args...) - the leading arguments bound, the rest forwarded - and C++23's std::bind_back binds the trailing arguments instead. It is the standard library's closest thing to a partially applied function factory and reads better than std::bind because there are no placeholders to keep in sync; it still holds the callable by value, so the lifetime and move rules are the same as for a capturing lambda.
pitfalls: bind_front binds the leading parameters only, which is the wrong end for data-last APIs - that case is what std::bind_back (C++23) exists for.
The wrapper stores the callable by value: binding a move-only callable moves it out of the original, which is gone afterwards.
